title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem
description: Learn how Dynamic Programming solves constrained optimization problems by maximizing value while respecting limited capacity constraints.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The **0/1 Knapsack Problem** is one of the most famous applications of Dynamic Programming involving optimal selection under constraints.

* Suppose a bag (knapsack) has a strict weight capacity.
* You are given several items, each with a specific `weight` and a specific `value`.
* The objective is to **maximize total value** without exceeding the bag's capacity.
* Each item can only be selected once (either 0 or 1 instances), which is why it is called "0/1" Knapsack.

Think of it like packing a suitcase for a trip. You have limited space measured by a weight limit. Each item provides a specific usefulness/value to you. You cannot take fractional items (you either pack your laptop or you don't), and you cannot take an item more than once.

This problem is fundamental in computer science because it strictly models constrained decision-making, where **Greedy Algorithms fail** and full Dynamic Programming 2D matrices are required.

sections.title: Why the Knapsack Problem Matters
sections.content:
Many real-world systems involve strictly limited resources combined with optimization goals. You want to maximize a benefit without breaking a hard limit.

Applications include:
1.  **Investment Planning:** Choosing which stocks to buy with a fixed capital limit to maximize expected portfolio return.
2.  **Logistics/Cargo:** Selecting which shipping containers to put on an airplane without exceeding takeoff weight limits.
3.  **Budget Optimization:** Choosing which corporate projects to fund given a fixed annual budget to maximize overall profit.
4.  **Server Allocation:** Assigning processing tasks to servers with capped CPU/memory capacity to maximize throughput.

The challenge is maximizing benefit while respecting limitations. Understanding the Knapsack algorithmic structure helps you design automated decision-making engines for all of these domains.
bullets: Introduces the foundational **2D Dynamic Programming matrix**.
Appears natively in **budgeting and logistics systems**.

sections.title: Problem Setup
sections.content:
Let us define the problem with concrete variables:
* **Capacity (`W`):** The absolute maximum weight the knapsack can hold (e.g., `4`).
* **Items:** Each has a `weight` and a `value`.
    * `Item A`: weight `1`, value `15`
    * `Item B`: weight `3`, value `20`
    * `Item C`: weight `4`, value `30`

Possible Selections:
* Take only `Item C`. Weight = 4. Value = **30**.
* Take `Item B`. Weight = 3. Value = **20**.
* Take `Item A` & `Item B`. Weight = `1 + 3 = 4`. Value = `15 + 20` = **35**.

The optimal solution is to take `A` and `B` for a value of 35. Notice that the best combination is *not* simply picking the single item with the highest value (`C=30`). You must evaluate combined sets.

sections.title: Why Greedy Selection Fails
sections.content:
A common beginner instinct is to use a Greedy algorithm. You might try picking the highest value item first, or the item with the best value-to-weight ratio. **Greedy fails completely for 0/1 Knapsack.**

* **Greedy by Highest Value:** If you pick `Item C` (Value=30, Weight=4), your remaining capacity is 0. Your final value is **30**. You missed the optimal `A+B` combo of **35**.
* **Greedy by Ratio:** 
    * `Item C` ratio = 30/4 = 7.5
    * `Item B` ratio = 20/3 = 6.66
    * `Item A` ratio = 15/1 = 15
    * Greedy by ratio picks `A` first (Weight=1, Cap=3 remaining). Next best ratio is `C` (doesn't fit). Next is `B` (Weight=3, Cap=0 remaining). In this specific instance ratio works, but it breaks easily on other datasets (e.g., if sizes prevent packing combinations cleanly).

Because items are discrete (0 or 1), greedy decisions trap the algorithm into wasting remaining capacity. DP solves this by safely tracking *all* possible optimal capacity utilization states.

sections.title: Core Dynamic Programming Idea
sections.content:
Dynamic Programming solves the Knapsack problem by generating solutions for smaller, hypothetical knapsacks (sub-capacities) and building up to the true capacity `W`.

* **Overlapping Subproblems:** The optimal packing configuration for "capacity 3 using only items A and B" will be referenced multiple times when deciding whether to add item C.
* **Optimal Substructure:** The optimal solution for capacity `W` using items `0..i` inherently relies on the optimal solution for capacity `W - weight[i]` using items `0..i-1`.

Instead of branching out into `O(2^n)` subsets recursively, DP uses a 2D matrix to record the best possible value for *every capacity from 0 to W*, factoring in one item at a time.

sections.title: Understanding the DP Matrix
sections.content:
The central structure in Knapsack DP is the **2D Matrix (`dp[i][w]`)**.

* **Rows (`i`):** Represent the items being considered (from 0 to `n`).
* **Columns (`w`):** Represent the hypothetical knapsack capacities (from 0 to `W`).
* **Cell Value:** `dp[i][w]` stores the absolute maximum value achievable using a subset of the *first `i` items* strictly constrained to *capacity `w`*.

**Base Cases:**
* `Row 0` (0 items available) = 0 value. Nothing to pack.
* `Column 0` (0 capacity available) = 0 value. Nothing fits.

As you evaluate row `i`, you introduce one new item to the system. You decide mathematically if including this new item is superior to excluding it. The final answer rests in the bottom-right corner: `dp[n][W]`.

sections.title: DP Matrix Visualization
sections.content:
Let's trace the matrix for Capacity = 4, Items = A(w:1, v:15), B(w:3, v:20), C(w:4, v:30).

1.  **Row 1 (Item A only):** Fits in all capacities `w >= 1`. Cells for `w=1` through `w=4` all get value `15`.
2.  **Row 2 (Items A & B):** 
    * For `w=1`, `w=2`, B doesn't fit. Value remains `15` (copied from above).
    * For `w=3`, B fits. Value `20` > `15`. Take `20`.
    * For `w=4`, B fits. Value of B (`20`) + Best value for remaining `w=1` (which is A=`15`). Total `35`. Take `35`.
3.  **Row 3 (Items A, B, & C):**
    * For `w=4`, C fits. Value of C (`30`) + Best value for remaining `w=0` (`0`). Total `30`.
    * Excluding C retains the value from above (`35`). 
    * `35 > 30`, so keep `35`.

The bottom right cell resolves to **35**.

sections.title: Decision-Making Per DP Cell
sections.content:
At every matrix cell `dp[i][w]`, the algorithm asks one binary question: **Include or Exclude the current item?**

* **Option 1: Exclude.** We don't pack item `i`. The maximum value is simply whatever the best value was for the same capacity `w` using only the previous items `i-1`. 
    * Value = `dp[i-1][w]` (the cell directly above).
* **Option 2: Include.** We pack item `i` (only allowed if `weight[i] <= w`). We gain `value[i]`, but we consume `weight[i]` capacity. We must add `value[i]` to the best optimal packing of the *remaining* capacity `w - weight[i]` using previous items.
    * Value = `value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]`.

The algorithm executes a pure `max()` check between Option 1 and Option 2.

sections.title: Knapsack Recurrence Relation
sections.content:
The mathematical core of Knapsack Dynamic Programming is this recurrence relation:

**If the item fits (`weight[i] <= w`):**
`dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]])`

**If the item does NOT fit (`weight[i] > w`):**
`dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]`

This recurrence drives the optimization process safely and reliably, comparing the "skip it" path against the "take it" path at every sub-capacity tier.

sections.title: Backtracking: Finding Which Items Were Selected
sections.content:
The bottom right cell `dp[n][W]` tells you the *maximum value*, but it doesn't immediately tell you *which items* you packed. To find the items, you trace back from `dp[n][W]`.

1.  Start at `i = n, w = W`.
2.  Compare `dp[i][w]` to the cell above it `dp[i-1][w]`.
3.  **If they are the SAME:** Item `i` was NOT included. Move UP to `i = i-1`.
4.  **If they are DIFFERENT:** Item `i` WAS included. Record Item `i`, subtract its weight from `w` (`w = w - weight[i]`), and move UP to `i = i-1`.
5.  Repeat until `i == 0` or `w == 0`.

For our example matrix ending in `35`:
* `dp[3][4] == 35`. Cell above `dp[2][4] == 35`. They match. Item C was skipped.
* `dp[2][4] == 35`. Cell above `dp[1][4] == 15`. Different! Item B was packed. `w` becomes `4 - 3 = 1`.
* `dp[1][1] == 15`. Cell above `dp[0][1] == 0`. Different! Item A was packed.
* Packed Items: **A and B**.

sections.title: Knapsack Loop Structure
sections.content:
The algorithm processes the matrix using nested standard loops:

1.  **Outer Loop:** Iterates over items `i` from `1` to `n`.
2.  **Inner Loop:** Iterates over capacities `w` from `0` to `W`.
3.  **Condition:** Check if `weight[i-1] <= w`.
4.  **Max Logic:** Apply the recurrence relation to set `dp[i][w]`.

This simple `O(n * W)` loop guarantees that every required subproblem is solved before it is needed by a larger subproblem.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content:
The 2D Dynamic Programming implementation uses nested lists in Python. 

* We create `dp = [[0] * (capacity + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]`.
* We use zero-indexing for the `weights` and `values` lists (`i-1`), while mapping `1` through `n` to the DP matrix rows.
* Because `w` represents the raw capacity integer, we can use it directly as an index.

codeSnippets.title: 0/1 Knapsack implementation
codeSnippets.code:
weights = [1, 3, 4]
values = [15, 20, 30]
capacity = 4
n = len(weights)

# Initialize DP matrix
dp = [[0 for _ in range(capacity + 1)] for _ in range(n + 1)]

for i in range(1, n + 1):
    for w in range(capacity + 1):
        if weights[i - 1] <= w:
            include = values[i - 1] + dp[i - 1][w - weights[i - 1]]
            exclude = dp[i - 1][w]
            dp[i][w] = max(include, exclude)
        else:
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w]

print("Maximum Value:", dp[n][capacity])

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
The algorithm processes every sub-capacity for every item.

* **Time Complexity:** `O(n * W)`, where `n` is the number of items and `W` is the knapsack capacity. 
* **Space Complexity:** `O(n * W)` for the full 2D DP matrix. (This can technically be space-optimized to `O(W)` by keeping only the two most recent rows, as row `i` only ever checks row `i-1`).

Is `O(n * W)` polynomial? Technically, it is **Pseudo-Polynomial** because it scales based on the numeric value of `W` rather than the size of the input elements. 

However, compared to the brute force `O(2^n)` subset generation, DP is miraculous. For `n=40`, brute force tests 1 trillion combinations. If `W` is 1000, DP performs just 40,000 checks—transforming an impossible lifetime computation into a millisecond task.

sections.title: Why Knapsack Strictly Requires DP
sections.content:
The Knapsack Problem sits mathematically right on the boundary where greedy techniques fail, forcing DP.

* **Greedy fails:** Because items cannot be fractionally divided (you can't take 50% of a laptop), packing a high-value bulky item might leave small amounts of wasted, unfillable space.
* **Overlapping Subproblems:** Computing the best loadout for "15 pounds remaining" happens repeatedly when testing different combinations of earlier items.
* **Optimal Substructure:** The optimal 50-pound loadout containing a 10-pound item fundamentally relies on finding the perfect 40-pound loadout among the remaining items.

DP evaluates *both* sides of the binary inclusion split (take it or leave it) and caches the results, completely shielding against greedy traps while avoiding exponential tree bloat.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Knapsack algorithms are deployed in any system with a strict "budget" ceiling:

* **Cloud Computing:** Assigning Virtual Machines (VMs) to physical server racks based on CPU limits to maximize client throughput.
* **Advertising Tech:** Selecting which targeted ads to bid on given a specific programmatic daily budget ceiling to maximize conversion rates.
* **Shipping & Logistics:** Loading Amazon delivery trucks with boxes of varying sizes to maximize delivery value per trip.
* **Fantasy Sports:** Drafting optimal Daily Fantasy rosters while staying under the team salary cap.

subsections.title: Mistake: Using greedy selection for 0/1 Knapsack
subsections.content: Greedy value/weight ratios do not produce optimal answers for 0/1 Knapsack because discrete shapes trap wasted space. You must evaluate the full DP matrix.

subsections.title: Mistake: Confusing 0/1 Knapsack with Fractional Knapsack
subsections.content: 0/1 Knapsack only allows complete selection or complete rejection. **Fractional Knapsack** allows taking 30% of an item (like loose gold dust), and for Fractional Knapsack, a Greedy value-to-weight ratio *does* mathematically work perfectly.

subsections.title: Mistake: Misunderstanding the DP matrix meaning
subsections.content: Cell `dp[i][w]` does *not* mean you MUST use item `i`. It means you are evaluating the absolute best loadout selecting from *any* of the items `0` through `i`.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: 0/1 Knapsack focuses on optimal discrete selection under a **hard constraint**.
Items must be taken entirely (1) or left entirely (0).
**Greedy selection fails** because discrete sizes trap wasted capacity.
Dynamic Programming uses a **2D matrix** to test all sub-capacities.
The algorithm runs in **`O(n * W)` time**, saving it from `O(2^n)` exponential death.
